secondaryCondition: Urge urinary incontinence (overactive bladder from diabetic neurogenic bladder dysfunction, with urgency, frequency and leakage) in a veteran with service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7542 (neurogenic bladder), rated as voiding dysfunction under § 4.115a, which supplies the urgency, frequency and urine-leakage tiers; where the predominant problem is sphincter or outlet dysfunction rather than the bladder itself, DC 7550 through DC 7556 address urethral and sphincter impairment and DC 7517 addresses urinary incontinence not otherwise classified. The evaluation must rest on documented voiding findings — measured post-void residual, urodynamic testing or a urology assessment of the leakage pattern — rather than on the symptom label, and DC 7542 must not be used to rate the same frequency and urgency findings that another genitourinary code already compensates. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus, with documented duration, glycaemic control and, to carry this theory, evidence of autonomic neuropathy
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7913 (diabetes mellitus), assigned on the insulin, dietary and activity-regulation tiers, with Note (1) requiring that compensable complications of diabetes be evaluated separately under their own codes unless they are already part of the 100-percent criteria. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Microvascular and autonomic-neuropathy sequence. Chronic hyperglycaemia in service-connected type 2 diabetes damages the small vessels and the autonomic nerve fibres that supply the lower urinary tract, and because bladder control depends on a coordinated reflex arc among bladder afferents, the pontine micturition centre, the sacral parasympathetic outflow to the detrusor and the sympathetic and pudendal outflow to the sphincters, any interruption of that arc produces a predictable set of disorders of storage and emptying rather than a single symptom. The functional consequences are, first, impaired afferent signalling, so that bladder filling is sensed late and the filling threshold shifts; second, detrusor overactivity, in which uninhibited contractions develop during filling and produce urgency and urge incontinence; and third, in the decompensated phase, an acontractile or underactive detrusor with impaired emptying and elevated post-void residual urine, which itself worsens urgency by reducing functional capacity and by promoting urinary tract infection. Urothelial dysfunction compounds the problem, because the urothelium is an active sensory organ whose purinergic and cholinergic signalling changes in diabetes, augmenting the afferent drive that generates urgency. Golbidi and Laher (PMID 21833175) describe diabetic cystopathy as a well-recognized complication of diabetes that usually develops in middle-aged or elderly patients with long-standing and poorly controlled disease, with a broad clinical spectrum running from overactive bladder and urge incontinence to decreased bladder sensation and overflow incontinence. Liu and Daneshgari (PMID 24709194) review diabetic bladder dysfunction and record both halves of the physiology: the classic picture of decreased bladder sensation, increased bladder capacity and impaired emptying with elevated post-void residual, and the more recent clinical and experimental recognition of a strong presence of storage problems such as urge incontinence in diabetes; they describe time-dependent phases in which an early compensatory phase is followed by a decompensated phase, identify a multifactorial pathophysiology involving the detrusor, the urothelium, the autonomic nerves and the urethra, and propose that polyuria produces bladder hypertrophy early while oxidative stress from chronic hyperglycaemia drives the later failure of bladder function. Agochukwu-Mmonu and colleagues (PMID 33197694) describe diabetic autonomic neuropathy as affecting the entire autonomic nervous system and producing genitourinary dysfunction that includes diabetic bladder dysfunction, sexual dysfunction and recurrent urinary tract infection, and they note that genitourinary complications of diabetes are very common — indeed more common than diabetic neuropathy or nephropathy as conventionally counted — with the UroEDIC study, an ancillary study of the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial and its Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications follow-up, demonstrating significant associations between cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy and urologic complications. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory. The service-connected diabetes is asserted to have produced a separate, separately rated genitourinary disability, and DC 7913's own note contemplates exactly that structure by directing that compensable complications be evaluated separately rather than absorbed into the diabetes rating. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory unless the record shows pre-existing non-service-connected urge incontinence — for example from childbirth and pelvic floor injury, prostate surgery or an unrelated neurological disease — antedating the diabetes, in which case the baseline level of severity must be established by medical evidence created before the onset of aggravation or by the earliest evidence created between onset of aggravation and the current evidence of severity, and both the baseline and any natural progression must be deducted from the current level. Chronology and evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the urge urinary incontinence is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected diabetes therefore require: (1) documented type 2 diabetes with duration and glycaemic history; (2) evidence of autonomic neuropathy or at least of the microvascular complication burden that makes the mechanism plausible, because the mechanism asserted here is neuropathy-mediated and a claim that rests on diabetes alone is a weaker claim; (3) objective documentation of the leakage pattern, that is, a urology or urogynecology assessment with measured post-void residual and, where performed, urodynamic findings of detrusor overactivity, rather than symptoms alone; and (4) exclusion or weighing of the competing causes below, with particular attention in men to bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia and in women to pelvic floor and obstetric history. Four candid limitations belong on the face of the opinion. First, a substantial part of the two-phase pathophysiological model — early compensatory hypertrophy followed by decompensation, with polyuria as the early driver and oxidative stress as the late driver — derives from animal models of type 1 diabetes, and Liu and Daneshgari state expressly that future clinical studies should investigate type 1 and type 2 diabetes separately and that animal studies of type 2 diabetic bladder dysfunction are needed; the model is therefore being applied across diabetes types and the opinion should say so. Second, the most detailed human cohort evidence on autonomic neuropathy and urologic complications comes from UroEDIC, a type 1 diabetes cohort, so the cohort-level association is established in the other diabetes type even though the anatomy, innervation and mechanism are shared. Third, the competing causes that must be excluded or weighed are numerous and common: in men, benign prostatic hyperplasia and other outlet obstruction, prostate cancer treatment and urethral stricture; in women, pelvic organ prolapse, obstetric and pelvic floor injury, menopause-related urogenital atrophy and prior pelvic surgery; in both, diuretic and anticholinergic or sympathomimetic medication effects, urinary tract infection, bladder stones or tumour, interstitial cystitis and bladder pain syndrome, spinal cord disease including disc disease and cauda equina syndrome, Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis, obesity, and high caffeine intake. Fourth, rating discipline under § 4.14 and the Note (1) to DC 7913 prevent the same genitourinary impairment from being compensated twice, and where more than one voiding code plausibly applies the schedule requires a single evaluation reflecting the predominant disability picture. No individual probability is asserted here; § 3.102 governs and the opinion must rest on documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes and an approximate balance of evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Bladder dysfunction in diabetes mellitus.
medicalEvidence.summary: Review describing diabetic cystopathy as a well-recognized complication that usually develops in middle-aged or elderly patients with long-standing and poorly controlled diabetes, with a clinical spectrum that runs from overactive bladder and urge incontinence to decreased bladder sensation and overflow incontinence, and setting out the pathophysiological mechanisms of the urologic complications of diabetes. Supplies the direct statement that overactive bladder with urge incontinence is part of the diabetic bladder phenotype.

medicalEvidence.title: Diabetic bladder dysfunction.
medicalEvidence.summary: Review contrasting the classic picture of decreased bladder sensation, increased capacity and impaired emptying with elevated post-void residual against the more recent clinical and experimental recognition of a strong presence of storage problems such as urge incontinence in diabetes, describing time-dependent compensatory and decompensated phases and a multifactorial pathophysiology of detrusor, urothelium, autonomic nerves and urethra, and attributing the early phase to polyuria and the later failure to oxidative stress from chronic hyperglycaemia. Also the source of an explicit limitation carried on the row, because it calls for type 1 and type 2 diabetes to be studied separately and notes the need for type 2 animal studies.

medicalEvidence.title: Autonomic neuropathy and urologic complications in diabetes.
medicalEvidence.authors: Agochukwu-Mmonu N; Pop-Busui R; Wessells H; Sarma AV
medicalEvidence.summary: Narrative review establishing that diabetic autonomic neuropathy affects the entire autonomic nervous system and produces genitourinary dysfunction including diabetic bladder dysfunction, sexual dysfunction and recurrent urinary tract infection, that genitourinary complications of diabetes are more common than diabetic neuropathy or nephropathy as conventionally counted, and that the UroEDIC study of the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial and its follow-up demonstrated significant associations between cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy and urologic complications. Links the autonomic lesion to the urologic outcome and — as a disclosed limitation — rests its cohort evidence in type 1 diabetes.

secondaryCondition: Tarsal tunnel syndrome (posterior tibial nerve entrapment at the ankle with plantar burning, numbness, night pain and neuropathic progression to sensory loss) in a veteran with service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8525 (posterior tibial nerve): 30 percent complete paralysis, 20 percent severe incomplete, 10 percent moderate and 10 percent mild, with DC 8625 (neuritis) as the alternative code where the presentation is predominantly inflammatory and painful and DC 8725 (neuralgia) where it is purely sensory pain; DC 8524 (internal popliteal nerve (tibial)) is the proximal comparator where the lesion lies above the tarsal tunnel, and the appropriate peripheral-nerve code must follow the documented distribution and severity rather than the diagnosis label. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus with documented duration and glycaemic history, and with the accrued sensory loss or polyneuropathy that the tarsal tunnel literature identifies as the setting in which entrapment produces its worst consequences
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7913 (diabetes mellitus), assigned on the insulin, dietary and activity-regulation tiers, with the note to DC 7913 addressing the separate evaluation of compensable complications including peripheral neuropathy, which is itself rated under its own code. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Metabolic and compressive nerve-injury sequence acting on the same nerve. The posterior tibial nerve passes through a fibro-osseous tunnel behind the medial malleolus formed by the flexor retinaculum and the medial surfaces of the talus and calcaneus, so it is anatomically vulnerable to compression, and its terminal branches supply the plantar surface of the foot. In diabetes the nerve is already injured by the metabolic and microvascular processes of diabetic neuropathy — hyperglycaemia-driven polyol pathway flux, accumulation of advanced glycation end-products, oxidative stress, endoneurial ischaemia from microangiopathy of the vasa nervorum and impaired axonal transport — which produces a swollen, mechanically vulnerable nerve with a widened cross-sectional area and a raised threshold to pressure. Compression superimposed on that substrate produces a focal entrapment neuropathy at the tunnel, and the two mechanisms compound rather than merely coexist: an already-damaged nerve tolerates compression less well, the epineurial and endoneurial oedema of diabetic neuropathy reduces the space within the fibro-osseous tunnel, and altered foot biomechanics — including the reduced ankle mobility and increased plantar pressures associated with diabetes and obesity — can add further traction and compression. The clinical result is plantar burning and numbness, pain that characteristically wakes the patient at night, a positive Tinel sign behind the medial malleolus, and progression to measurable sensory loss with impaired plantar protective sensation, which in turn raises the risk of diabetic foot ulceration and amputation. Rinkel and colleagues (PMID 30113445) evaluated 240 subjects with diabetes without neuropathy and 176 diabetic subjects with neuropathy from the prospective Rotterdam Diabetic Foot Study together with 196 non-diabetic controls, found a positive Tinel sign at the tarsal tunnel to be a valid discriminator of tibial nerve abnormality, and reported the prevalence of tibial nerve entrapment as 44.9 percent (95 percent confidence interval 40.1 to 49.7 percent) in diabetic patients versus 26.5 percent (95 percent confidence interval 20.3 to 32.7 percent) in healthy controls (p less than 0.0001), concluding that the significantly more frequent neuropathic complaints and sensory disturbances provide evidence for the role of superimposed entrapment neuropathy in diabetes-related neuropathy. Rinkel and colleagues (PMID 32276769), in the same prospective cohort, compared 113 subjects with tarsal tunnel syndrome against 303 diabetic controls without it and found that incident diabetic foot ulceration occurred in 17.4 percent (95 percent confidence interval 8.4 to 26.3 percent) of subjects with bilateral tarsal tunnel syndrome versus 8.3 percent (95 percent confidence interval 5.1 to 11.6 percent) of controls (p equals 0.0036), with diminished sensation at the hallux independently increasing ulceration risk in patients with prior ulceration (hazard ratio 4.692, p equals 0.003) and without it (hazard ratio 2.307, p equals 0.002), and concluded that elevated sensory thresholds in tarsal tunnel syndrome render diabetic patients at higher risk of foot ulceration and that with effective surgery it is likely to be an amenable factor in preventing diabetic foot disease. Abo Omirah and colleagues (PMID 40591366) studied 34 patients presenting with tarsal tunnel syndrome and found a significant association between body mass index, HbA1c level and age with severity both clinically on the Takakura scale and electrophysiologically on Mondelli's scale, with higher body mass index and elevated HbA1c strongly associated with greater severity and a high prevalence of bilateral involvement. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory in which the service-connected diabetes is asserted to have produced a separate, separately rated focal neuropathy at the tarsal tunnel, evaluated under its own peripheral-nerve code rather than folded into the diabetes or generalised-neuropathy rating. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory unless the record shows pre-existing non-service-connected tarsal tunnel syndrome — from an old ankle fracture, a previous ankle sprain or surgery, or a structural cause such as a tarsal coalition — antedating the diabetes, in which case the baseline level of severity must be established by medical evidence created before the onset of aggravation or by the earliest evidence created between onset of aggravation and the current evidence of severity, and the baseline and any natural progression must be deducted. Chronology and evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the tarsal tunnel syndrome is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected diabetes therefore require: (1) documented type 2 diabetes with duration and glycaemic history; (2) a clinical description of the plantar pain, burning or numbness with a localising examination including a Tinel sign at the tarsal tunnel and a documented sensory distribution that follows the posterior tibial nerve and its plantar branches rather than the symmetric glove-and-stocking pattern of generalised diabetic polyneuropathy; (3) electrodiagnostic confirmation or another objective localising study, because elicitation of a positive Tinel sign is a screening finding and not by itself a diagnosis; and (4) exclusion or weighing of the competing causes below. Four candid limitations belong on the face of the opinion. First, two of the three anchors come from the same prospective cohort and the same research group, so they are not independent corroboration of the same proposition, and the practitioner should treat the 44.9 percent figure as a single-cohort estimate rather than a replicated constant. Second, the third anchor is a single-centre cross-sectional study of only 34 patients, so it can support a severity gradient but not an incidence statement. Third, the ordinal question is real and must be addressed on the record: diabetic polyneuropathy itself produces plantar numbness and burning, so the examiner has to show that the findings localise to the tarsal tunnel rather than merely being part of generalised neuropathy, which is the same distinction the anchors draw between entrapment and polyneuropathy and which is the point of obtaining focal conduction studies. Fourth, the competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include diabetic distal symmetric polyneuropathy itself, lumbosacral radiculopathy at the S1 level, plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinopathy and retrocalcaneal pathology, peripheral arterial disease, hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency including that induced by metformin, alcohol-related neuropathy, monoclonal gammopathy and other paraproteinaemias, tarsal coalition and accessory musculature, prior ankle trauma or surgery with scarring, chronic ankle oedema and venous insufficiency, and obesity with altered foot biomechanics. Rating discipline under § 4.14 prevents the same sensory loss from being compensated twice under a peripheral-nerve code and again as generalised diabetic neuropathy, and the schedule requires a single evaluation for the predominant disability picture. No individual probability is asserted here; § 3.102 governs and the opinion must rest on documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes and an approximate balance of evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Validity of the Tinel Sign and Prevalence of Tibial Nerve Entrapment at the Tarsal Tunnel in Both Diabetic and Nondiabetic Subjects: A Cross-Sectional Study.
medicalEvidence.authors: Rinkel WD; Castro Cabezas M; van Neck JW; Birnie E; Hovius SER; Coert JH
medicalEvidence.summary: Cross-sectional analysis within the prospective Rotterdam Diabetic Foot Study of 240 diabetic subjects without neuropathy, 176 diabetic subjects with neuropathy and 196 non-diabetic controls found a positive tarsal-tunnel Tinel sign to be a valid discriminator of tibial nerve abnormality and reported tibial nerve entrapment prevalence of 44.9 percent (95 percent confidence interval 40.1 to 49.7 percent) in diabetic patients versus 26.5 percent (20.3 to 32.7 percent) in controls (p less than 0.0001), concluding that superimposed entrapment neuropathy contributes to diabetes-related neuropathy. The row discloses that this and the following anchor come from the same cohort and group.

medicalEvidence.title: The natural history of tarsal tunnel syndrome in diabetic subjects.
medicalEvidence.authors: Rinkel WD; Castro Cabezas M; Birnie E; Coert JH
medicalEvidence.summary: Comparing 113 subjects with tarsal tunnel syndrome against 303 diabetic controls, incident diabetic foot ulceration occurred in 17.4 percent of those with bilateral tarsal tunnel syndrome versus 8.3 percent of controls (p equals 0.0036), with diminished hallux sensation independently increasing ulceration risk (hazard ratio 4.692 with prior ulceration, p equals 0.003; 2.307 without, p equals 0.002). Establishes that the entrapment has measurable downstream consequences — the feature that makes it a compensable disability rather than a laboratory finding.

medicalEvidence.title: The Association between Body Mass Index, HbA1c Levels, and Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome: A Clinical and Neurophysiological Study.
medicalEvidence.authors: Abo Omirah MH; Kamal M; Gomaa M; Ewais AA; AlRasheed HA; Bahaa MM; Thabet S; Moawad HM; Magdy MM
medicalEvidence.summary: Single-centre cross-sectional study of 34 patients with tarsal tunnel syndrome found a significant association between body mass index, HbA1c level and age with severity on both the clinical Takakura scale and Mondelli's electrophysiological severity scale (p less than 0.05), with higher body mass index and elevated HbA1c strongly associated with greater severity and a high prevalence of bilateral involvement. Supports a glycaemic-severity gradient; the row discloses its small single-centre sample so the finding cannot be used as an incidence statement.

secondaryCondition: Complex regional pain syndrome (post-stroke shoulder-hand syndrome phenotype, with regional pain, oedema, vasomotor, sudomotor and trophic change and associated upper-limb disuse) following service-connected residual neurologic deficit after stroke
secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated complex-regional-pain-syndrome diagnostic code is listed in 38 CFR Part 4. A clinically justified analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 is required, selected on the documented distribution, pain intensity, vasomotor, sudomotor and trophic findings and the functional loss they produce, so the code must follow the findings rather than the diagnostic label. The word causalgia appears in § 4.124a only as descriptive language inside DC 8525 (posterior tibial nerve) and is not asserted here as an automatic comparator, and where the dominant impairment is loss of use of the affected upper limb the musculoskeletal or amputation-principles provisions govern instead. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected residual neurologic deficit after ischemic or haemorrhagic stroke (status post cerebrovascular accident), with documented motor deficit, spasticity or sensory disturbance
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8007 (embolism), DC 8008 (thrombosis) or DC 8009 (haemorrhage): the vascular conditions of the brain are rated 100 percent for six months following the ictus and thereafter on residuals with a minimum evaluation of 10 percent, and residual motor or sensory findings are separately evaluated under the appropriate neurological or musculoskeletal provisions. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Post-stroke neuropathic pain sequence with peripheral and central components, compounded by hemiplegic disuse. A stroke that damages the corticospinal and sensory pathways and their cortical targets does not merely paralyse the limb; it leaves the affected upper limb in a state in which nociceptive and sympathetic control is disordered, and the region can then generate a self-sustaining pain state in the shoulder, wrist and hand rather than pain confined to the site of any single lesion. The mechanisms that have been described are convergent. Locally there is an exaggerated inflammatory response with release of chemical mediators into the tissue around primary afferent fibres, the so-called inflammatory soup, which lowers the activation threshold of nociceptors and produces peripheral sensitisation; this accounts for the oedema, vasodilation and sweating disturbance of the early phase. Repeated discharge of C fibres then increases the excitability of dorsal horn and higher neurons, producing central sensitisation, and reorganisation of the primary somatosensory cortex follows, so that the pain is maintained by central mechanisms even when the peripheral inflammatory stimulus has settled. The role of the sympathetic nervous system is now in doubt rather than assumed, although a subgroup of patients appears to have sympathetic hyperactivity and to respond to sympathetic blockade. Post-stroke complex regional pain syndrome is recognised as arising in the setting of the hemiplegic upper limb, and its onset and severity track the characteristics of the stroke itself, including the aetiology of the stroke, the severity and degree of recovery of the motor deficit, spasticity, sensory disturbance and glenohumeral subluxation. Katsura and colleagues (PMID 36281309) studied 102 patients with first-ever stroke and found a prevalence of post-stroke complex regional pain syndrome of 18.6 percent (19 of 102), with significantly worse Fugl-Meyer Assessment, Action Research Arm Test and Motor Activity Log scores in the affected group, Fugl-Meyer and Action Research Arm Test scores correlating with pain intensity, Motor Activity Log scores almost zero, and the conclusion that post-stroke pain syndrome may be influenced by the degree of upper limb inactivity after stroke. Pertoldi and Di Benedetto (PMID 16474282) reviewed shoulder-hand syndrome after stroke and describe complex regional pain syndrome types I and II as neuropathic pain disorders developing as an exaggerated response to a traumatic lesion or nerve damage, generally affecting the extremities, or as the consequence of a distant process such as stroke, spinal lesion or myocardial infarction; they set out the peripheral sensitisation, central sensitisation and cortical reorganisation mechanisms described above, record that the central role of the sympathetic nerve is presently in doubt except in a subgroup that responds to sympathetic block, note that the onset and severity of shoulder-hand syndrome appear related to the aetiology of the stroke and to the severity and recovery of the motor deficit, spasticity, sensory disturbances and glenohumeral subluxation, and state that the diagnosis is clinical with no specific or pathognomonic test. Kim and colleagues (PMID 27495051) add an important competing account: in a prospective observational study of 23 patients with post-stroke complex regional pain syndrome they found ultrasonographic swelling of the extensor digitorum communis tendon at the affected wrist, a significant reduction in tendon cross-sectional area, wrist swelling and visual analogue scale score after steroid injection at that tendon (all p less than 0.001), and concluded that the pathophysiology of post-stroke complex regional pain syndrome may be a combination of frozen shoulder or rotator cuff tear of the shoulder with soft-tissue injury of the wrist caused by the hemiplegic state. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory in which the service-connected residual stroke deficit is asserted to have produced a separate, separately rated pain condition with its own evaluation by analogy, rather than being absorbed into the rating for the paralysis itself. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory unless the record shows pre-existing complex regional pain syndrome from an earlier non-service-connected injury — a distal radius fracture, a prior stroke or a shoulder injury — antedating the service-connected stroke, in which case the baseline level of severity must be established by medical evidence created before the onset of aggravation or by the earliest evidence created between onset of aggravation and the current evidence of severity, and the baseline together with any natural progression must be deducted. Chronology and evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the complex regional pain syndrome is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected stroke residuals therefore require: (1) documented stroke with its residual motor, spasticity or sensory deficit; (2) clinical findings satisfying the accepted diagnostic criteria for complex regional pain syndrome applied to the affected limb — disproportionate pain, oedema, vasomotor or sudomotor change, trophic change and functional limitation — with a description of the distribution rather than a bare diagnosis, because there is no pathognomonic test and the diagnosis is clinical; (3) objective corroboration where available, including three-phase bone scan, magnetic resonance imaging or ultrasonographic findings and the response to a clinician-directed intervention, while recognising that these support rather than establish the diagnosis; and (4) a chronology in which the pain syndrome develops after the stroke rather than before it, together with exclusion or weighing of the competing causes below. Four candid limitations belong on the face of the opinion. First, the diagnosis is clinical and has no confirmatory test, so the principal competing diagnoses must be excluded on the record and not merely dismissed: these include adhesive capsulitis and rotator cuff pathology of the hemiplegic shoulder, which the Kim anchor identifies as a plausible alternative or additional mechanism, cervical radiculopathy, compressive neuropathy such as carpal tunnel syndrome, spasticity-related pain, heterotopic ossification, deep vein thrombosis with post-thrombotic swelling, cellulitis, gout or crystal arthritis, shoulder subluxation pain, and diabetic or other peripheral neuropathy. Second, the mechanism is genuinely contested — the sympathetic contribution is doubted in the general case, central and peripheral mechanisms are both invoked, and one located anchor attributes a substantial part of the syndrome to shoulder and wrist soft-tissue injury in the hemiplegic limb — so the opinion should assert the recognised association between stroke and the pain syndrome and the individual's own findings, and should not claim that a single established mechanism has been proved in that veteran. Third, the prevalence found in the located cross-sectional study, 18.6 percent, is a single-centre estimate in first-ever stroke patients and cannot be substituted for an individual causation conclusion. Fourth, rating discipline under § 4.14 prevents the same pain, oedema or loss of function from being compensated twice, in particular once as residuals of the stroke and again as complex regional pain syndrome, and where the limb findings overlap the schedule requires a single evaluation reflecting the predominant disability picture. No individual probability is asserted here; § 3.102 governs and the opinion must rest on documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes and an approximate balance of evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Shoulder-hand syndrome after stroke. A complex regional pain syndrome.
medicalEvidence.summary: Review describing complex regional pain syndrome types I and II as an exaggerated response to a traumatic lesion or nerve damage or as the consequence of a distant process such as stroke, spinal lesion or myocardial infarction; setting out peripheral sensitisation, central sensitisation and cortical reorganisation as the mechanisms; recording that the central role of the sympathetic nerve is presently in doubt except in a subgroup responding to sympathetic block; and stating that onset and severity of shoulder-hand syndrome relate to the stroke aetiology, the severity and recovery of the motor deficit, spasticity, sensory disturbance and glenohumeral subluxation, with diagnosis remaining clinical and having no pathognomonic test.

medicalEvidence.title: Is poststroke complex regional pain syndrome the combination of shoulder pain and soft tissue injury of the wrist?: A prospective observational study: STROBE of ultrasonographic findings in complex regional pain syndrome.
medicalEvidence.authors: Kim YW; Kim Y; Kim JM; Hong JS; Lim HS; Kim HS
medicalEvidence.summary: Prospective observational study of 23 patients with post-stroke complex regional pain syndrome found ultrasonographic swelling of the extensor digitorum communis tendon at the affected wrist and a significant reduction in tendon cross-sectional area, wrist swelling and visual analogue scale score after steroid injection at that tendon (all p less than 0.001), concluding that the syndrome may be a combination of frozen shoulder or rotator cuff tear with soft-tissue injury of the wrist caused by the hemiplegic state. Cited here for the treatment-response dimension and — candidly — as the competing mechanical hypothesis that the row requires an examiner to address.

medicalEvidence.title: Post-Stroke Complex Regional Pain Syndrome and Upper Limb Inactivity in Hemiplegic Patients: A Cross-Sectional Study.
medicalEvidence.authors: Katsura Y; Ohga S; Shimo K; Hattori T; Yamada T; Matsubara T
medicalEvidence.summary: Cross-sectional study of 102 patients with first-ever stroke reported a prevalence of post-stroke complex regional pain syndrome of 18.6 percent (19 of 102), with significantly worse Fugl-Meyer Assessment, Action Research Arm Test and Motor Activity Log scores in affected patients, Fugl-Meyer and Action Research Arm Test scores correlating with pain intensity, and almost zero Motor Activity Log scores, concluding that the syndrome may be influenced by the degree of upper-limb inactivity after stroke. Supplies the prevalence bound and the disuse component on the face of the row.

secondaryCondition: Neurogenic heterotopic ossification (ectopic lamellar bone forming in the soft tissues around the hip, elbow or other joints, with pain, restricted motion and possible ankylosis) complicating service-connected traumatic brain injury residuals
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5023 (heterotopic ossification); the note to DCs 5013 through 5024 directs that group to be evaluated as degenerative arthritis on limitation of motion of the affected parts, so the evaluation follows the affected joint's limitation-of-motion criteria, with § 4.59 governing painful motion where motion is relatively preserved, § 4.56 governing muscle evaluation, and the ankylosis criteria of the affected joint applying where ankylosis develops. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected residuals of traumatic brain injury, with a documented closed-head, blast or penetrating injury and persistent physical residuals
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8045 (residuals of traumatic brain injury), evaluated on its cognitive-impairment and subjective-symptom tables with separate evaluation of physical residuals in the affected body system. Note that § 3.310(d) supplies a presumption of proximate result only for a closed list of sequelae — parkinsonism, unprovoked seizures, certain dementias, depression and diseases of hormone deficiency — and heterotopic ossification is not on that list, so no presumption is claimed and this row proceeds on individual causation evidence. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Neurogenic osteogenic sequence after central nervous system injury. Heterotopic ossification is the formation of true lamellar bone within soft tissue outside the skeleton, and the neurogenic form arises in a characteristic pattern around the large joints of patients who have sustained a traumatic brain injury or spinal cord injury. The current understanding is that central nervous system injury creates a permissive and then a directive environment for endochondral bone formation: local tissue hypoxia and inflammation after the injury recruit and activate mesenchymal progenitor cells, altered sympathetic and neuropeptide signalling modifies the local vascular and inflammatory milieu, and circulating humoral factors released after brain injury promote osteogenic differentiation and osteoblast activity, so that the same injury that destroys neurological function also up-regulates the bone-formation programme. Mechanical and local factors contribute independently, because the ectopic bone forms preferentially where soft tissue is compressed, immobilised or repeatedly loaded, and the hip and elbow are the classic sites. Sullivan and colleagues (PMID 23610702) state that neurogenic heterotopic ossification is a disorder of aberrant bone formation affecting one in five patients sustaining a spinal cord injury or traumatic brain injury, that ectopic bone forms around joints in characteristic patterns causing pain and limiting movement especially around the hip and elbow, that its clinical sequelae include urinary tract infection, pressure injuries, pneumonia and poor hygiene, and that pathophysiological understanding derives from basic bone-formation mechanisms enhanced by evidence of systemic influences from circulating humoral factors and perhaps neurological ones, with prophylaxis and treatment based on non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, bisphosphonates, radiation therapy and surgery. Simonsen and colleagues (PMID 17572418) studied an approximately complete consecutive series of 114 adult patients with very severe traumatic brain injury treated in a specialised brain injury unit against the prospectively registered Danish National Head Injury database combined with radiographs obtained for heterotopic ossification symptoms or fracture control, and found clinically significant heterotopic ossification in 7.9 percent of patients, with logistic regression showing an independent significant positive correlation with female sex and a high Injury Severity Score; they attributed the comparatively low incidence to early mobilisation and physiotherapy and observed that the higher incidence among women speaks for humoral and hormonal factors initiating bone formation outside the bones. Huang and colleagues (PMID 29662775) reviewed the relationship between heterotopic ossification and traumatic brain injury and record that ectopic lamellar bone forms in soft tissues, that postnatal heterotopic ossification is usually induced by fracture, burn, neurological damage including brain and spinal cord injury, or joint replacement, that patients who sustain a bone fracture combined with severe traumatic brain injury are at significantly increased risk, and that brain damage promotes bone formation while the exact mechanisms remain to be clarified. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory in which the service-connected traumatic brain injury residuals are asserted to have produced a separate, separately rated skeletal condition at its own diagnostic code, DC 5023, rather than being absorbed into the residuals rating. It is not a § 3.310(d) presumption case, because heterotopic ossification does not appear on the closed list of sequelae presumed to be the proximate result of service-connected traumatic brain injury, and the opinion should say so expressly rather than imply a presumption. It is equally not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory unless the record shows pre-existing heterotopic ossification from an earlier non-service-connected cause — an old fracture, a burn, joint replacement or a previous spinal cord injury — antedating the service-connected injury, in which case the baseline level of severity must be established by medical evidence created before the onset of aggravation or by the earliest evidence created between onset of aggravation and the current evidence of severity, and the baseline and any natural progression must be deducted. Chronology and evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the heterotopic ossification is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected traumatic brain injury therefore require: (1) a documented traumatic brain injury with its mechanism and severity, because injury severity is an identified independent correlate of the condition; (2) imaging that demonstrates the ectopic bone and its relation to the joint, since plain radiographs may lag the clinical onset by weeks and a three-phase bone scan or other functional imaging may be required to identify the lesion early; (3) a clinical description of the pain, localised swelling, warmth, reduced joint range and, where relevant, ankylosis, with the resulting functional loss quantified by range-of-motion measurement; and (4) a chronology in which the ossification appears after the injury, characteristically weeks to months afterwards, together with exclusion or weighing of the competing causes below. Four candid limitations belong on the face of the opinion. First, the reported incidence of heterotopic ossification after traumatic brain injury ranges widely in the literature and the two located quantitative anchors bracket that range from opposite directions — one in five overall for the combined spinal cord and brain injury population and 7.9 percent for clinically significant disease in a very severe brain injury cohort with early mobilisation — so no single percentage may be presented as this veteran's probability, and this row discloses both. Second, humoral and hormonal causation is inferred rather than demonstrated in the individual: the female predominance and the association with injury severity are epidemiological observations and the mechanism remains, in the words of the located review, to be clarified. Third, the competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include trauma-induced heterotopic ossification from an associated fracture, which commonly coexists in the same patient and requires apportionment rather than a global attribution to the brain injury; burns; prior joint replacement; spinal cord injury if present, which is a distinct clinical entity in the catalogue and must be evaluated on its own basis rather than merged with the brain injury; myositis ossificans traumatica; dystrophic or metastatic calcification; osteochondroma and other primary bone lesions; fracture callus; periosteal reaction from infection; and tumour calcinosis. Fourth, rating discipline under § 4.14 prevents the same limitation of motion from being compensated twice — once as the joint's own injury and again as heterotopic ossification — and because the note to DCs 5013 through 5024 requires evaluation on limitation of motion of the affected parts, an examiner whose findings are limited to pain with preserved motion must address § 4.59 explicitly rather than leaving the impairment uncompensated by silence. No individual probability is asserted here; § 3.102 governs and the opinion must rest on documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes and an approximate balance of evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Heterotopic ossification after central nervous system trauma: A current review.
medicalEvidence.authors: Sullivan MP; Torres SJ; Mehta S; Ahn J
medicalEvidence.summary: Review establishing that neurogenic heterotopic ossification is a disorder of aberrant bone formation affecting one in five patients sustaining a spinal cord injury or traumatic brain injury, that ectopic bone forms around joints in characteristic patterns causing pain and limiting movement especially around the hip and elbow, that its sequelae include urinary tract infection, pressure injuries, pneumonia and poor hygiene, and that the pathophysiology stems from basic bone-formation mechanisms enhanced by systemic humoral and possibly neurological influences. The primary incidence-and-mechanism anchor for this row.

medicalEvidence.title: Symptomatic heterotopic ossification after very severe traumatic brain injury in 114 patients: incidence and risk factors.
medicalEvidence.authors: Simonsen LL; Sonne-Holm S; Krasheninnikoff M; Engberg AW
medicalEvidence.summary: Consecutive series of 114 adults with very severe traumatic brain injury, drawn from a prospectively registered national head-injury database and radiographs, found clinically significant heterotopic ossification in 7.9 percent overall, with logistic regression showing an independent significant positive correlation with female sex and a high Injury Severity Score; the authors attribute the low incidence to early mobilisation and physiotherapy and read the female predominance as evidence of humoral and hormonal factors in bone formation outside the skeleton. Supplies the severity-of-injury correlate and the lower bound of the reported incidence range.

medicalEvidence.title: Relationship between heterotopic ossification and traumatic brain injury: Why severe traumatic brain injury increases the risk of heterotopic ossification.
medicalEvidence.authors: Huang H; Cheng WX; Hu YP; Chen JH; Zheng ZT; Zhang P
medicalEvidence.summary: Review recording that heterotopic ossification is ectopic lamellar bone in soft tissue, that postnatal heterotopic ossification is usually induced by fracture, burn, neurological damage including brain and spinal cord injury, or joint replacement, and that patients with bone fracture combined with severe traumatic brain injury are at significantly increased risk; it summarises the osteogenic and humoral changes described after severe brain injury and states that brain damage promotes bone formation while the precise mechanisms remain to be clarified. Supplies the biological-plausibility step and, candidly, the admission that the mechanism is not fully established.

secondaryCondition: Xerostomia (persistent dry mouth with salivary hypofunction, oral discomfort, altered taste, difficulty swallowing dry foods, denture intolerance and increased caries risk) from maintenance inhaled anticholinergic therapy in a veteran with service-connected chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated diagnostic code for xerostomia or salivary hypofunction is listed in 38 CFR Part 4. A clinically justified analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 is required, based on demonstrated oral dryness, salivary measurement where available and the functional impact; where the dryness is an inseparable burden of the service-connected respiratory treatment it may instead be evaluated with the respiratory condition, and where the predominant impairment is of swallowing the digestive or the appropriate neurological provisions apply. No diagnostic code is invented here. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected chronic obstructive pulmonary disease treated with a maintenance inhaled anticholinergic agent such as tiotropium or ipratropium
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.97, DC 6604 (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), rated on forced-expiratory-volume and diffusion-capacity thresholds with a 100-percent evaluation available where the disease is severe or requires outpatient oxygen therapy, and with the residuals of treatment separately considered where the schedule so provides. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Antimuscarinic pharmacology acting on the salivary glands, augmented by the route of administration. Inhaled anticholinergic bronchodilators such as tiotropium and ipratropium relax bronchial smooth muscle by blocking muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, and their therapeutic selectivity is relative rather than absolute: the same M3 receptor population that mediates bronchoconstriction also mediates parasympathetic stimulation of salivary secretion, so receptor blockade in the salivary glands reduces both the watery serous output of the parotid glands and the mucinous output of the submandibular and minor glands. Salivary flow is not a trivial function; it lubricates and clears the oral mucosa, buffers acid, delivers antimicrobial proteins and calcium and phosphate for enamel remineralisation, and conditions food for swallowing, which is why its loss produces the cluster of complaints seen in xerostomia — persistent oral dryness with a sticky or burning sensation, altered taste, intolerance of dry foods and of dentures, fissuring of the lips and tongue, and accelerated dental caries. Two features of the inhaled route make the effect more likely and more local than the same drug given systemically. First, a substantial fraction of an inhaled dose is deposited in the oropharynx rather than in the lung, so the salivary and mucosal receptors of the mouth and pharynx are exposed to a high local concentration of drug, which is the same oropharyngeal exposure that produces the recognised oral complications of inhaled therapy. Second, the drug's duration at the receptor determines whether the effect is transient or continuous, and the long-acting agents are designed to occupy the receptor for a full dosing interval, so a once-daily maintenance inhaler can produce continuous rather than intermittent dryness. The effect is a class effect of the antimuscarinic mechanism and is not limited to the airway: the pooled trial data show that the same drug class also increases the risk of urinary retention, which is a second manifestation of the identical pharmacological action. Casaburi and colleagues (PMID 11083677) randomised 470 patients with stable COPD (mean forced expiratory volume in one second 38.6 percent of predicted) to tiotropium 18 micrograms once daily or placebo for three months and found that the most commonly reported adverse event after tiotropium was dry mouth, at 9.3 percent versus 1.6 percent for placebo (p less than 0.05). Kesten and colleagues (PMID 17166984) pooled adverse-event data from 19 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled tiotropium trials comprising 4,435 tiotropium patients and 3,384 placebo patients contributing 2,159 and 1,662 person-years of exposure, found dry mouth to be among the four most commonly reported events, and reported a materially increased relative risk of dry mouth in the tiotropium group (relative risk 3.60, 95 percent confidence interval 2.56 to 5.05), together with an increased relative risk of urinary retention (relative risk 10.93, 95 percent confidence interval 1.26 to 94.88). Xu and colleagues (PMID 39403528) analysed 75,899 dry-mouth adverse-event reports from the United States Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System between the first quarter of 2004 and the first quarter of 2024 using four disproportionality methods and found that tiotropium bromide monohydrate was the single drug most frequently reported for dry mouth (2,080 cases), while the five drugs with the highest reporting odds ratios were all antimuscarinic agents (darifenacin, solifenacin, fesoterodine, tolterodine and niraparib), and noted that eight of the top nineteen drugs causing dry mouth were not flagged for that effect in their labelling. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory carried through treatment, because the disability is asserted to be proximately due to the medication prescribed for the service-connected chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and the medication is the proximate instrument rather than the lung disease itself. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory unless the record shows pre-existing xerostomia from a non-service-connected cause antedating the inhaler therapy, in which case the baseline level of severity must be established by medical evidence created before the onset of aggravation or by the earliest evidence created between onset of aggravation and the current evidence of severity, and both the baseline and the natural progression of that pre-existing condition must be deducted. The distinction between the two theories matters clinically here, because a veteran whose mouth was already dry from Sjögren's syndrome, head and neck radiotherapy or another anticholinergic medication has a § 3.310(b) claim for the increment only, whereas a veteran whose oral function deteriorated after a maintenance inhaler was started has a § 3.310(a) claim for the condition itself, and the two require different evidence. Chronology and evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the xerostomia is at least as likely as not caused by the inhaled anticholinergic prescribed for the service-connected lung disease therefore require: (1) documentation of the chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and of the specific inhaler with its dose and start date, taken from pharmacy records rather than from recollection; (2) the prescribing indication, since the treatment-mediated chain runs to the service-connected respiratory condition only while that condition is the reason the drug was prescribed; (3) objective documentation of reduced salivary function rather than the complaint of dryness alone — a clinical description of the oral mucosa with, where available, sialometry, a salivary flow assessment or an objective measure of oral dryness, because self-reported dry mouth correlates imperfectly with measured hypofunction; and (4) a temporal relationship in which the dryness begins with or after the inhaler was started and improves or resolves when it is stopped or changed, with cessation or substitution decided by the treating clinician and never by the examiner or the veteran on their own initiative. Four candid limitations belong on the face of the opinion. First, two of the three anchors are sponsored trial analyses rather than independent research, and the authors of the pooled safety analysis are affiliated with the manufacturer of the drug in question, so the row leans on the pharmacovigilance analysis for independent confirmation and discloses the conflict of interest rather than presenting the trial data as unconflicted. Second, xerostomia is extremely common in the general and ageing population, so an opinion that does not exclude the ordinary causes cannot rise above possibility; those competing causes include other antimuscarinic and anticholinergic medications that are extremely common in a veteran population — urinary antispasmodics, tricyclic antidepressants, first-generation antihistamines, antipsychotics, antiparkinson agents, muscle relaxants and some antiemetics — as well as Sjögren's syndrome and other autoimmune disease, poorly controlled diabetes, head and neck radiotherapy, salivary gland disease including sialolithiasis and sialadenitis, chronic graft-versus-host disease, viral infection including HIV and hepatitis C, dehydration, mouth breathing, smoking and alcohol use, anxiety, and positive-pressure therapy for sleep-disordered breathing. Third, the oral manifestations of inhaled therapy are not all xerostomia: inhaled corticosteroids, which are frequently combined with the long-acting bronchodilator in a single inhaler, cause oral candidiasis and dysphonia, and a veteran with oral discomfort may have candidiasis rather than true salivary hypofunction, so the examiner must distinguish the mucosal infection from dryness and must not attribute to the anticholinergic what the corticosteroid or the infection produced. Fourth, there is no dedicated diagnostic code for this disability, so evaluation proceeds by analogy under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 and rating certainty is limited even where service connection is sound; rating discipline under § 4.14 also prevents the same treatment-related impairment from being compensated twice, and the veteran should not be told a fixed rating attaches to the diagnosis. No individual probability is asserted here; § 3.102 governs and the opinion must rest on documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes and an approximate balance of evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Pooled clinical trial analysis of tiotropium safety.

medicalEvidence.title: Disproportionality analysis of drug-induced dry mouth using data from the United States food and drug administration adverse event reporting system database.
